<reason>PRO built its case around a single natural experiment (Bracero's expansion, abolition, and the enforcement era) and defended it through every round: it directly answered CON's scale question with Bracero's order-of-magnitude growth, and its closing timeline point (removals ended mid-decade, apprehensions stayed low until the program ended) plausibly blunted CON's Operation Wetback rescue. PRO also pinned a real concession ("leaves the stock of jobs-for-smugglers untouched") into a clean decision rule about demand. CON's strongest material—compliance depends on enforcement scaffolding, and expansion manufactures a queue of rejected applicants—was sharp and partially unanswered, but its 1986 IRCA example was an amnesty rather than a seasonal work channel, which PRO correctly flagged as off-motion, and CON's "recruits" claim in closing was asserted rather than shown. PRO's clipped turn was a minor cost. Overall PRO made the comparative question easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Rebuttal 2: CON demanded a seasonal program that scaled while keeping returns high, and PRO answered with Bracero's growth to hundreds of thousands of admissions during the very years apprehensions collapsed, directly contradicting CON's "no version survives contact with scale." CON's Operation Wetback counter was then weakened by PRO's timeline reply in closing.</best_rebuttal>
